case_studies.title: CARI: Cross-Boundary Adversarial Runtime Injection in Coding-Agent Workflows
case_studies.abstract: Coding agents increasingly develop, test, and integrate software whose components are owned by different developers, teams, or services. This exposes a distinct attack surface: a malicious or compromised peer development role can manipulate a live component of the software under development (e.g., a backend service, test harness, CI job, or deployment service) and influence the runtime feedback that another role's coding agent must process to complete its task. Although such a component has legitimate diagnostic authority to report its own state, it has no action authority over the victim's local files, credentials, shell, or development environment. We introduce Cross-Boundary Adversarial Runtime Injection (CARI), a direct runtime-feedback injection setting that exploits this authority mismatch. Rather than explicitly compromising the victim's prompt, model, tools, or local environment, the attacker covertly embeds malicious instructions in task-relevant runtime feedback produced by a peer-controlled development component. The victim then interprets that feedback as part of normal debugging or recovery, and may translate the diagnostic guidance into unauthorized victim-side actions. We instantiate ten different attacks based on CARI, spanning resource exhaustion, information exposure, and development-state manipulation. Across four programming languages and five code-capable models, CARI succeeds in 2,845/3,000 (94.8%) trials. Furthermore, CARI transfers effectively to product-level coding agents, achieving 61.3% attack success on Codex and 58.7% on Claude Code. By contrast, prompt-level defenses exhibit a security-utility trade-off: generic warnings are ineffective, whereas explicit policies suppress attacks but substantially over-refuse legitimate actions.
case_studies.summary: CARI shows that a compromised development component can inject malicious instructions into the runtime feedback of coding agents, leading to resource exhaustion, data leaks, or state changes. The researchers built ten attacks across multiple languages and models, achieving up to 94.8% success, and proved the technique works on real product agents like Codex and Claude Code. This is relevant to cloud infra managers because insecure CI/CD or deployment services could become the injection vector.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage CI/CD or deployment services that provide runtime feedback to development agents, check that the feedback cannot be tampered with by other services; isolate feedback channels and validate authenticity before agents act on them.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel attack vector (CARI) relevant to security of coding agents used in modern CI/CD pipelines, directly impacting infrastructure engineers who deploy and manage such systems. The research is theoretical with no released tool, so maturity is low. However, the findings can inform actionable security testing services and tool enhancements, giving moderate monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: Understanding and Mitigating Role Spoofing in LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Despite growing capabilities, LLMs remain susceptible to prompt injections: malicious inputs that can manipulate or hijack models. In particular, it has recently been observed that LLMs can exhibit role confusion (Ye et al., 2026), where models attribute the source of text based on its style instead of its labeled role. Malicious text in tool outputs (for instance, a malicious webpage accessed by an agent) can leverage role confusion to impersonate the user, an attack we call role spoofing}. In this work, we seek to understand and mitigate role spoofing. We study how models track "who said what" in a conversation, showing that they use cues from both content (e.g., semantics and writing style) and structure (e.g., control tokens and formatting). We show that LLMs are highly susceptible to role spoofing attacks that combine both fake structure and content. Additionally, in a toy setting, we show that adversarial training which teaches the model to ignore content-based injections does mitigate content-based attacks but leaves the model susceptible to structure-based attacks. This can explain why frontier models, with increased resistance to many injection attacks, can still be susceptible to role spoofing. Finally, we propose a new method for detecting role spoofing using linear probes trained to predict roles in a conversation, and show that it is effective across different settings.
case_studies.summary: This study shows that large language models can be tricked into attributing text to the wrong role (role spoofing) by mixing fake structure and content cues, making them vulnerable to hijacking attacks. The researchers built a detection method using linear probes that reliably flags spoofed roles across different model settings. For IT infrastructure managers, the work highlights a new security risk with LLM‑powered tools but does not directly change day‑to‑day cloud ops.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑enabled services, implement role‑spoof detection: 1) add a linear probe layer to your inference pipeline that flags anomalous role assignments; 2) audit prompt templates to ensure control tokens are unforgeable; 3) train models with adversarial examples that mix fake structure and content to harden against spoofing attacks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a security issue relevant to LLM-based agents and APIs used in enterprise settings, giving a moderate real-world impact. The solutions are largely experimental and not yet deployed, so maturity is low. However, the detection method could be packaged as a security service for SaaS or cloud platforms within a short time, giving a moderate monetisation potential.
